record.paper_title: Selected Open Problems in Discrete Geometry and Optimization
record.original_question: For a simple arrangement A_{d,n} of n hyperplanes in dimension d, where any d hyperplanes intersect at a distinct point, call the d-dimensional polyhedra defined by the hyperplanes the cells and call the bounded facets of an unbounded cell external. Let Phi_A(d,n) be the minimum number of external facets over all simple arrangements defined by n hyperplanes in dimension d. For n > d >= 3, is Phi_A(d,n+1) >= Phi_A(d,n) + Phi_A(d-1,n), and in dimension 3 is equality attained as Phi_A(3,n) = n^2 - 3n + 4 for all n >= 6?

evidence.quote: An arrangement A d,n of n hyperplanes in dimension d is simple if any d hyperplanes intersect at a distinct point. The d-dimensional polyhedra defined by the hyperplanes of an arrangement A d,n are called the cells of A d,n. The bounded facets of an unbounded cell are called external. Let Phi_A(d,n) be the minimum number of external facets for any simple arrangement defined by n hyperplanes in dimension d.

Question 5. We hypothesize that Phi_A(d,n+1) >= Phi_A(d,n) + Phi_A(d-1,n) for n > d >= 3, and that the inequality is satisfied with equality for d = 3 and n >= 6, i.e., Phi_A(3,n) = n2 - 3n + 4 for n >= 6.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $d \ge 2$ and $n \ge d$ be integers. An arrangement $\mathcal{A}_{d,n}$ of $n$ affine hyperplanes in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is called simple if any $d$ of the hyperplanes intersect in a single point and no $d+1$ of them share a common point. The connected components of the complement of the union of the hyperplanes are full-dimensional polyhedra called the cells of $\mathcal{A}_{d,n}$; a cell is unbounded if it is not a bounded set. A facet of a cell (a $(d-1)$-dimensional face contained in one of the hyperplanes) is called external if it is bounded and is a facet of some unbounded cell. Define 
$$\Phi_{\mathcal{A}}(d,n) = \min \{\, \text{number of external facets of } \mathcal{A}_{d,n} : \mathcal{A}_{d,n} \text{ is a simple arrangement of } n \text{ hyperplanes in } \mathbb{R}^d \,\}.$$

Prove or disprove the following two statements:

(a) For all integers $d \ge 3$ and $n > d$,
$$\Phi_{\mathcal{A}}(d, n+1) \;\ge\; \Phi_{\mathcal{A}}(d, n) + \Phi_{\mathcal{A}}(d-1, n).$$

(b) For $d = 3$ and every integer $n \ge 6$, the inequality in (a) holds with equality, and moreover
$$\Phi_{\mathcal{A}}(3, n) = n^2 - 3n + 4.$$
artifact.status_search_result: Web searches did not return any source that establishes the conjectured recurrence or the closed-form value $\Phi_{\mathcal{A}}(3,n)=n^2-3n+4$. The problem is posed as a hypothesis in the original problem collection on discrete geometry and optimization, and no subsequent resolution was found, so it appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Counting External Facets of Simple Hyperplane Arrangements (CiteSeerX)
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses counting and minimizing external facets of simple hyperplane arrangements; notes that the line arrangement minimizing external facets also maximizes the average diameter, but this is not known to extend to higher dimensions.
status_evidence.claim: Background work on counting/minimizing external facets exists, but no result establishing the conjectured recurrence or closed-form value was found.
